note: Fish cards for the Learn page. Every fact comes from the official page named in that card's 'source' (checked on 't'); a section is left out when that page does not give it. Size, bag and season are never kept here: they come from the rules data for the chosen state.

points: Releasing a fish while it stays in the water is the safest option.
If you must lift a fish out of the water, wet your hands first to protect its slime.
A landing tool such as a lip grip helps control the head and reduces damage to the gills and eyes.
For a photo, keep the fish horizontal and support its full weight.
If a fish looks lethargic when released, move water gently through its mouth and over its gills (use the current, or move the fish in a figure-8).
Dehooking tools shorten handling time. If a fish is gut-hooked, cut the line as close to the hook as possible.
Reef fish caught deeper than about 50 feet can suffer barotrauma. Use a descending device or venting tool only when the fish shows signs of it, and use it quickly.

fish.name: Snook
fish.appearance: Large mouth with a lower jaw that sticks out past the upper jaw, a sloped forehead, a tall dorsal fin split into sections, a black lateral line that runs onto the tail, and yellow pelvic fins.
fish.size: Up to 48 inches (50 pounds).
fish.habitat: Inshore coastal waters: mangrove shorelines, seagrass beds, beaches and areas around structure.
habits: Snook start life as males; some become females at roughly 18 to 22 inches.
They form schools in spawning season.
They eat fish and large crustaceans.
They cannot survive water colder than 60°F, and they can tolerate fresh water.
fish.when: They face moving water and wait for prey to be carried down the current.
baits: Live pinfish, small mullet, shrimp or sardines
rigs: Free-lined, or fished off the bottom with a fish finder rig
tips: Snook jump clear of the water and burst into long runs.
They take a large variety of lures, depending on water conditions.
Beware of the razor-sharp gill covers.

fish.name: Tarpon
fish.appearance: Dark blue-green or greenish-black back becoming bright silver on the sides, one dorsal fin whose last ray stretches into a long filament, very large scales, and a large mouth that points upward.
fish.size: Up to 8 feet (300 pounds).
fish.habitat: Primarily inshore fish; adults spawn offshore. They are found along Florida's coast in summer and concentrate in South Florida in winter as coastal water cools.
habits: Slow-growing; they mature at 7 to 13 years of age.
They spawn between May and September.
They tolerate a wide range of salinity, and juveniles are commonly found in fresh water.
They gulp air at the surface and feed on fish and large crustaceans.
baits: Flies, streamers, lures, jigs, and live or dead bait (tackle depends on the bait, the place and the size of the fish)
tips: Tarpon are powerful, explosive, acrobatic fighters with great stamina.
A long, heavy monofilament leader is very important to protect your line from the gill plate and tail.
Tarpon have poor food value and are almost exclusively a catch-and-release fishery.
A tarpon tag must be bought in advance to keep one, and only in pursuit of a Florida state record.

fish.name: Redfish (red drum)
fish.appearance: Copper-bronze body fading to a lighter belly; one or more dark spots at the base of the tail (occasionally none); no chin barbels; large scales.
fish.size: Up to 61 inches.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters. In winter, redfish are found in seagrass; they also use muddy or sandy bottoms, oyster bars and spring-fed creeks.
habits: Juveniles stay inshore until about 30 inches (about 4 years old), then join the nearshore population.
Spawning runs roughly August through December in passes, inlets and lagoon estuaries.
They make a drumming sound by vibrating muscles against the air bladder.
They eat fishes and invertebrates.
baits: Live shrimp
Crabs, mullet, pinfish and killifish (mud minnows)
Soft-bodied jigs, spoons and topwater plugs
rigs: Live shrimp floated under a popping cork
tips: One of Florida's most popular sport fish and its most widespread estuarine fish.
fish.lookalikes: Black drum have chin barbels and no spot on the tail.

fish.name: Spotted seatrout
fish.appearance: Back dark gray or green fading to a silvery or white belly; several black spots on the back reaching the dorsal fins and tail; a pair of large canine teeth at the tip of the upper jaw; no chin barbels. Also known as speckled trout.
fish.size: Up to 39 inches (17 pounds); common to 14 inches.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters over sand bottoms or seagrass beds.
habits: Spawning happens inshore from March through November.
In colder months they move into deeper, still waters.
They eat baitfish, mullet, shrimp and crabs.
baits: Live shrimp, or small pinfish or pigfish (grunts), free-lined near the bottom to draw trout out of grass-bed holes
Soft-bodied jigs, topwater poppers and spoons
rigs: A float lets the bait drift over grass beds while you search for trout
tips: Trout are fragile: release unwanted or illegal fish quickly to keep the population healthy.
fish.lookalikes: Weakfish have irregular wavy lines instead of spots.

fish.name: Flounder
fish.appearance: A bottom-oriented flatfish with both eyes on the left side. Many spots and blotches, plus three dark eye-like spots in a triangle; strong canine-like teeth; a wedge-shaped tail. (This card is the Gulf flounder.)
fish.size: Common to 14 inches (2 pounds).
fish.habitat: Inshore on sandy or mud bottoms; often moves into tidal creeks and occasionally is caught over nearshore rocky reefs.
habits: The right eye migrates to the left side early in life.
It lives on the bottom and is thought to spawn offshore.
It eats crustaceans and small fish.
It can change color to match its surroundings.
fish.lookalikes: Southern flounder may have five or more spots, but they are not eye-like. Summer flounder has five or more eye-like spots.

fish.name: Sheepshead
fish.appearance: Also called convict fish: light body with vertical black bars, prominent incisor, molar and grinder teeth, no barbels on the lower jaw, and strong sharp fin spines.
fish.size: Up to 36 inches; common to 13 inches.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters near structure such as oyster bars, seawalls and tidal creeks. They move nearshore in late winter and early spring to spawn.
habits: Fractional spawners, laying part of their eggs at a time inshore, typically in March and April.
Omnivores, feeding mostly on crustaceans and small fish.
baits: Live shrimp, sand fleas or fiddler crabs
rigs: A small hook fished on the bottom
tips: When cleaning, beware of the sharp gill covers.
fish.lookalikes: Black drum have chin barbels and lack incisor-like teeth. Atlantic spadefish lack incisor-like teeth.

fish.name: Black drum
fish.appearance: Highly arched gray or black back fading to a lighter belly; juveniles have 4 to 6 dark vertical bars that fade with age; barbels on the lower jaw; large scales; powerful throat teeth that crush oysters.
fish.size: Up to 67 inches.
fish.habitat: Inshore fish found in bays, river mouths and lagoons. Bottom dwellers, often around oyster beds, docks and bridge pilings; they may also be offshore, and juveniles live in estuaries.
habits: The largest of the drum species.
They spawn nearshore in winter and early spring.
They eat fishes and invertebrates, including oysters, mussels, crabs and shrimp.
They live 35 years or more.
baits: Cut bait, shrimp, sand fleas or blue crabs
tips: Keeping the bait on the bottom where they feed is very important.
Bait-casting or spinning gear with 15 to 30 lb line suits most conditions.
fish.lookalikes: Red drum and sheepshead lack lower-jaw barbels. Juvenile black drum bars somewhat resemble those on sheepshead and spadefish.

fish.name: Florida pompano
fish.appearance: Dark greenish-gray back shading to silver sides, with a yellowish belly; fish from dark waters have yellow on the throat, pelvic and anal fins. A deep, compressed body with a small mouth and a gently sloping forehead.
fish.size: Up to 24 inches (8 pounds).
fish.habitat: Inshore and nearshore waters, especially along sandy beaches, oyster bars and over seagrass beds, often in turbid water; found as deep as 130 feet.
habits: They spawn offshore from March to September.
They feed on mollusks and crustaceans, especially sand fleas.
Local movements are influenced by the tide, and seasonal movements by temperature.
fish.lookalikes: Permit: the dorsal fin begins over the anal fin, and permit grow much larger than Florida pompano.

fish.name: Spanish mackerel
fish.appearance: Bluish-green back, silvery sides and belly, irregular golden-yellow spots, a bluish-black blotch on the front of the first dorsal fin, and a lateral line that slopes gently.
fish.size: Up to 36 inches.
fish.habitat: Prevalent throughout Florida waters: inshore, offshore and nearshore, often over grass beds and reefs. They are absent from north Florida waters in winter.
habits: Schooling fish that migrate north in spring and return south when water drops below 70°F.
They spawn offshore from spring through summer.
They feed on small fishes and invertebrates.
baits: Small shiny spoons, dusters or jigs, trolled or cast
tips: They are aggressive and strike many natural and artificial baits.
Look for birds diving on baitfish: mackerel are likely driving bait to the surface.
Light spinning or bait-casting gear with 10 to 15 lb monofilament is adequate.
Use a 30 to 60 lb monofilament leader because of their razor-sharp teeth.
fish.lookalikes: Cero has a yellowish stripe on its sides. King mackerel's lateral line drops sharply below the second dorsal fin.

fish.name: Bluefish
fish.appearance: Blue-green back and silvery sides and belly, with a prominent jaw and sharp, compressed teeth.
fish.size: Grow fast to as much as 31 pounds and 39 inches.
fish.habitat: Along the East Coast from Maine to eastern Florida. Adults live inshore and offshore and prefer warmer water; juveniles prefer sandy bottoms. They form size-based schools that can cover tens of square miles.
habits: They eat squid and fish, especially menhaden and silversides; in feeding blitzes they attack baitfish near the surface and eat almost anything they can catch and swallow.
Females spawn several times in spring and summer; eggs are released in the open ocean.
They migrate north in spring and summer as the water warms, and south in autumn and winter.
They live up to 12 years.
tips: Recreational harvest peaks May through October, with over 70 percent of the catch in July and August.
Bluefish can accumulate mercury and PCBs, and some states recommend limited consumption.

fish.name: Mahi (dolphin)
fish.appearance: Bright greenish-blue back with yellow on the sides, able to flash purple, chartreuse and other colors; one dark dorsal fin from above the eye to the tail; a body that tapers sharply. Adult males have a nearly vertical head; females have a more sloping one.
fish.size: Up to 63 inches (88 pounds); common to 30 pounds.
fish.habitat: Offshore in warm waters. Young live in floating sargassum weed.
habits: A fast swimmer and one of the fastest-growing fish, thought to live no more than 5 years.
They spawn in warm oceanic currents for much of the year.
They eat flying fish, squid and other small fish while cruising weed lines.
baits: Natural baits such as ballyhoo
Artificial lures, feathers or spoons
rigs: Trolled ballyhoo on #7 or #8 steel wire with a 7/0 or 8/0 hook
tips: When one fish in a school is hooked, the rest often stay nearby.
Chumming with cut bait brings them in and creates a frenzy.
fish.lookalikes: Pompano dolphinfish have a square-shaped tooth patch on the tongue; dolphinfish have an oval one.

fish.name: Kingfish (king mackerel)
fish.appearance: Bluish-green back fading to silvery sides and belly, with no spots; no dark blotch on the front of the first dorsal fin; a lateral line that drops sharply below the second dorsal fin. Juveniles may have yellowish spots.
fish.size: Up to 72 inches.
fish.habitat: Coastal to offshore waters, often around piers; occasionally in deep water.
habits: They spawn offshore in mid-summer.
Schooling fish that winter in south Florida and migrate north in spring.
They feed mainly on fishes.
baits: Live pogies, herring, Spanish sardine, ballyhoo or mullet
Flashy sub-surface lures or large fish-like plugs
rigs: 20-pound line and tackle, or heavier for larger kings, with a wire or mono leader
Trolling with live bait works well (FWC Saltwater Fishing Tips)
tips: Kings feed on small fish and squid and take both natural and artificial baits.
fish.lookalikes: Cero and Spanish mackerel both have gently sloping lateral lines and a dark blotch on the front of the first dorsal fin. Wahoo has a long, continuous first dorsal fin.

fish.name: Cobia
fish.appearance: A long, slim fish with a broad, depressed head; also called ling or lemonfish. Brown with a whitish belly and a dark stripe from the eye to the tail; the lower jaw extends past the upper. Young fish have alternating black and white stripes.
fish.size: Up to 6 feet (150 pounds); common from 10 to 50 pounds.
fish.habitat: Nearshore and inshore waters, including inlets and bays, often near buoys, pilings and wrecks.
habits: They spawn in spring and early summer.
They eat crabs, squid and small fish.
baits: Live crabs and small fish
tips: Keep the bait near the surface or, if cobia are deeper, add just enough weight to get the bait down and still let it move.
Medium to heavy tackle is needed; these fish average 30 pounds.
fish.lookalikes: The remora has a sucker disk on top of its head.

fish.name: Red snapper
fish.appearance: Pinkish-red body fading to a white belly, a long triangular snout, a red eye and a pointed rear anal fin. Adults have no dark spot on the sides.
fish.size: Up to 36 inches (35 pounds).
fish.habitat: Adults are found offshore near structure; juveniles live over sand or mud bottoms.
habits: Spawning occurs from June to October.
They reach maturity at age 2 and can live more than 20 years, possibly up to 60.
They eat crustaceans and fish.
baits: Soft-bodied jigs, bucktails and spoons
fish.lookalikes: Silk snapper has a yellow eye. Vermilion snapper has a rounded anal fin.

fish.name: Mangrove snapper
fish.appearance: Also called mangrove snapper or mango. Dark brown to gray with red-orange spots in bars along the sides, two large canine teeth at the front of the upper jaw, and an anchor-shaped patch of teeth on the roof of the mouth. Young fish have a dark stripe from the snout through the eye.
fish.size: Common to 24 inches (10 pounds); gray snapper caught offshore are commonly 8 to 10 pounds.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters near structure such as reefs, mangroves and seagrass. Juveniles may enter fresh water.
habits: They spawn June through August.
They feed on crustaceans and small fish.
fish.lookalikes: Cubera snapper has a triangular tooth patch and grows much larger. Schoolmaster has yellow fins and faint white bars.

fish.name: Yellowtail snapper
fish.appearance: Olive to bluish back with yellow spots, a yellow stripe from mouth to tail that widens toward the rear, a yellow deeply forked tail, and narrow pink and yellow stripes on the lower sides.
fish.size: Up to 30 inches (5 pounds).
fish.habitat: Nearshore ocean waters, mainly around coral reefs.
habits: Mostly found in tropical waters.
They spawn in mid-summer.
They eat fishes and invertebrates.

fish.name: Gag grouper
fish.appearance: Brownish-gray with dark worm-like markings on the sides, a strong serrated spur on the cheek, dark fins with white edges on the anal fin and tail, and dark lines radiating from the eyes.
fish.size: Up to 36 inches (50 pounds); common to 25 pounds.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters near structure such as rocky bottoms, reefs and drop-off walls in water over 60 feet deep. Juveniles are found in estuaries and seagrass beds.
habits: Born as females but can later become male.
They spawn between January and May.
They feed on fishes and invertebrates.
Goliath and Nassau grouper are protected from harvest in Florida waters.
baits: Live fish, or dead cut or whole bait
rigs: Baits fished near the bottom with heavy tackle
fish.lookalikes: Black grouper: the spur on the cheek is gently rounded, not serrated.

fish.name: Greater amberjack
fish.appearance: Olive green or brownish back with silver sides; a dark stripe from the nose to the front of the dorsal fin that shows more when the fish is feeding; no scutes (bony projections).
fish.size: Up to 60 inches (176 pounds); common around 40 inches and under 40 pounds.
fish.habitat: Offshore around rocky reefs, debris and wrecks, usually in 60 to 240 feet of water; occasionally nearshore in South Florida. Juveniles associate with floating objects.
habits: The largest of the jacks.
Thought to spawn offshore for most of the year.
They feed on squid, fish and crustaceans.
baits: Almost any lively baitfish: blue runners, pinfish, pigfish, grunts, cigar minnows, sand perch
rigs: Just enough weight to keep the bait in the middle of the water column (amberjack swim above the reef)
tips: Anglers typically use 50- to 100-pound tackle, though lighter gear works in many situations.
When excited, they will surface and strike topwater plugs, jigs, spoons and diving lures.
They are very strong fighters with great endurance: set the drag in advance.

fish.name: Striped bass

source.label: NOAA Fisheries species profile: Atlantic Striped Bass

fish.appearance: Stout body with seven to eight continuous horizontal stripes on each side from gills to tail; light green, olive, steel blue, black or brown on top, with a white or silver underside.
fish.size: Can grow up to 5 feet and 77 pounds.
fish.range: Native from the St. Lawrence River in Canada to the St. Johns River in Florida, and in the Gulf from Florida to Louisiana. Introduced to inland lakes, reservoirs and the West Coast.
fish.habitat: Anadromous: they live in the ocean but return to fresh or brackish water to spawn. Juveniles usually stay in estuaries for 2 to 4 years. Some adults spend most of their lives in rivers or coastal estuaries; others live in the ocean.
habits: Adults are fish-eaters that take almost any small fish, plus crabs and squid.
Mature fish move to fresh or brackish water in spring to spawn.
Males mature at about 2 to 4 years; females at about 4 to 8 years.
They live up to 30 years.
tips: Federal waters (3 to 200 miles offshore) are closed to recreational fishing for this species.
State-water recreational fishing uses minimum sizes, bag limits and seasonal closures.

fish.name: Largemouth bass

source.label: FWC species profile: Florida Bass / Largemouth Bass

fish.appearance: The upper jaw extends beyond the rear edge of the eye, and the first and second dorsal fins are separated by a deep dip. Florida bass is now a separate species from largemouth bass, but the two are managed as one for regulations.
fish.habitat: Found statewide in lakes and rivers, usually near vegetation or underwater structure; schooling bass also appear in the middle of lakes.
habits: Black bass spawn in spring; males prepare a bed and guard the eggs and fry.
Young bass eat zooplankton, and at about an inch long begin eating other small fish.
Adults eat a variety of fish, crustaceans and larger insects.

fish.name: Bluegill
fish.appearance: A deep body like other bream, a long dorsal fin and a slightly forked tail; a dark ear cover and a blotch at the back bottom edge of the dorsal fin set them apart.
fish.habitat: Common throughout Florida, but best known in lakes and ponds.
habits: Bluegill mainly eat insects and their larvae.
They spawn all summer and gather in large beds; anglers may spot 30 to 40 shallow nests dug into sandy areas.
baits: Live worms or crickets, fished on the bottom or under a float
Crickets, grubs, sand maggots or grass shrimp for bedding bluegill
A 1/8 oz beetle spin with a white or chartreuse body on ultralight tackle
rigs: A small #6 or #8 hook with a split shot about 6 inches up the line
tips: Concentrate on water less than 6 feet deep.

fish.name: Black crappie
fish.appearance: A deep body with a speckled pattern on the body and fins.
fish.habitat: Unlike most other panfish, crappie spend much of their time offshore. They feed on small fish in lakes or in large, slow-moving, clear-water rivers.
habits: They nest in colonies from February to April; males fan nests over gravel or muddy bottoms at depths of 3 to 8 feet, and larger fish nest deeper.
Their main foods are crustaceans, aquatic insects and small fishes.
baits: Missouri minnows or grass shrimp below a float
A bright 1/16 to 1/8 oz jig or Hal-flies when they move inshore to spawn
rigs: A #4 hook with a small split shot, under a float
tips: Specks are a cool-weather favorite.
Depth is key because crappie school at the same level.

fish.name: Channel catfish
fish.appearance: Whisker-like barbels and a forked tail, rounded anal fins and scattered black spots on the back and sides. Males turn especially dark in spawning season and develop a thickened pad on the head.
fish.habitat: Found throughout Florida; they spawn in holes and crevices.
habits: Primarily bottom feeders, though they also feed higher in the water column.
Their major foods are aquatic insects, crayfish, mollusks, crustaceans and fish, not decaying material.
fish.when: Most active around dusk and during the night.
baits: Strong-smelling baits such as chicken liver or gizzards, shrimp, cut mullet and commercial stinkbaits
rigs: A sturdy #2 to #4 hook and a heavy split shot sinker, fished near the bottom
tips: Handle them carefully because their spines are sharp.

fish.name: Walleye

source.label: Minnesota DNR: Walleye biology and identification

fish.appearance: Torpedo-shaped, dark olive brown to yellowish gold, often with brassy flecks. The eye reflects light. The dorsal fin has no spots except a dark splotch at its rear base, and the lower tip of the tail is white.
fish.size: Averages 1 to 2 pounds in most waters and occasionally exceeds 10 pounds.
fish.habitat: In Minnesota, thrives in large, shallow, windswept lakes with gravel shoals, and is also native to many smaller lakes and streams.
habits: A fish-eater that relies heavily on yellow perch, which see poorly in low light and are easy prey at night.
They spawn over rock, rubble and gravel in rivers or windswept shallows 1 to 6 feet deep; spawning peaks at 42 to 50°F.
fish.when: They feed in shallow water at dawn and dusk. In daylight they move to shadows from cliffs, boulders, logs or heavy weeds, or to deeper water. They stay active longer in the day when turbidity, waves or clouds reduce light, and in summer spend more time in deep, cool water.
tips: Fishing may be poor when forage-size perch are abundant, because walleye are well fed.
fish.lookalikes: Sauger are smaller and more slender, have rows of dark spots on the dorsal fin, and lack the white tail tip.

fish.name: Rainbow trout

source.label: USGS NAS species profile: Rainbow Trout

fish.appearance: A deep-bodied, compressed fish with a typical trout shape, a moderately large head and a mouth reaching behind the eyes. Color varies a lot. Spots cover the back and reach about two-thirds of the way to the lateral line, and the sides are largely unspotted. Juveniles are olive-green with 8 to 13 oval marks along the sides.
fish.range: Native to the Pacific Slope from the Kuskokwim River in Alaska to at least Baja California, the upper Mackenzie River drainage, and basins in southern Oregon.
habits: Fish that leave lakes to spawn show more intense coloring: pinkish sides and fins turn crimson and the spots become bolder.
The ocean-going form is called steelhead.
